newsitem.title: UK: Gold relies on physical buying but price may fall.
newsitem.headline: Gold relies on physical buying but price may fall.

text.p: Physical buying might have supported the gold price at around $340.00 per ounce last week but the market's tendency was to move lower, bullion dealers said.
"It's just drifting and there is no real reason to buy it just now," one dealer said, noting the "summery" feel coming into gold trading and the orderliness of the major financial markets.
More immediately, London is on holiday on Monday and Tokyo activity will be curtailed as Japan celebrates Golden Week.
Gold hung around the $340.00 level all last week after forecasts that it would plumb the depths of four-year lows (at $336.90, hit on February 12) and possibly fall even further.
A fall of $2 to $3 at the beginning of the week was set up by selling following the expiry of options in London the previous Friday.
"The options players had been keep the price above $340 for their own purposes. When they started selling, the $340 went quickly," one dealer said.

However, fairly neutral outcomes from the meetings of the G7 and the International Monetary Fund/World Bank followed by a string of inflation-benign U.S.data last week took some of the downside pressure off gold.
"Apart from the yen, which has a little problem, currencies are looking good and inflation is under control. The G7 seems to be in control," a dealer said.

"Furthermore, the stock market is in good shape after correcting and recovering. Anybody who wanted out of there will have done so," the dealer added, noting that the stock market moves had had little lasting influence on the gold price.
Dealers said the bias was towards lower prices.
One bullion market source said the "gravitational pull" towards the four-year low would be difficult to resist.
"The temptation is to try the downside," one dealer said.
He noted that the South African gold miners' quarterly results which came out in the past couple of weeks were poor in most cases.
"An assault on the downside could provoke the South Africans into panic selling," the dealer warned.

The outlook for the other precious metals was more mixed. Silver was seen more closely tied to gold than to platinum and palladium, and was expected to encounter heavy selling if it got beyond $4.80 per ounce.
Platinum and palladium were still mainly supported by tight supplies resulting from the failure of Russia and Japan to open substantive talks on their long delayed 1997 supply contracts.
No metal has flowed from Russia, the largest exporter of palladium, to Japan, the biggest user of both metals, since December, pushing up and sustaining their prices.
"The Russian story is getting a bit stale now but until something happens there, you don't want to be short of either metal," a dealer said.
